analysis.one_liner: Reinstates the corporate environmental tax that funds Superfund toxic-waste cleanups.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and sat there until Congress ended, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have revived an expired corporate income tax — 0.12% on the taxable income of the largest corporations — with the revenue dedicated to the Superfund, the federal program that cleans up the nation's worst abandoned toxic-waste sites. The tax lapsed in 1995, shifting more cleanup costs onto regular taxpayers. The bill never got any action beyond being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near Superfund sites and ordinary taxpayers generally: reinstating the tax restores the 'polluter pays' principle, so companies responsible for contaminated sites (and the chemical and petroleum industries, which draw on the fund for cleanup liability) would help pay for cleanups rather than general taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the environmental income tax under Section 59A of the tax code, applying it to corporate taxable years from enactment through 2014, restoring a dedicated funding stream for the Superfund program [S3].
The tax is an income-based levy on corporations, meaning the burden falls on companies rather than on general taxpayers, supporting the polluter-pays principle for toxic-site cleanup [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations, especially chemical and petroleum companies, would pay the reinstated 0.12% environmental tax on their taxable income.

drawbacks.text: A corporate environmental tax is ultimately passed through to some combination of shareholders, workers, and consumers, and critics of Superfund taxes argued the fund should be paid for by general revenue since identifying responsible parties at old sites is difficult [S3].

The bill extends only the corporate environmental income tax under Section 59A, not the separate per-barrel and per-ton excise fees on crude oil and hazardous chemicals, so it would restore only part of the original polluter-pays funding structure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost to any single corporation is modest relative to profits, while the benefit is dedicated funding for cleaning up sites that threaten public health and that otherwise drain general taxpayer money. The main design weakness is partial: it leaves out the per-unit excise fees that once made polluters pay more directly.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 2, 2005, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
The committee took no further action, and no vote was ever held in either chamber [S5].
The bill drew no cosponsors during its life in Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations — especially chemical and petroleum companies — that would have paid the reinstated Superfund tax, and whose cleanup contributions instead continued to fall on general taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that avoided the cleanup tax

for.name: Rep. Sherwood Boehlert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on it, but drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 2, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting the bill die.

against.name: Chemical and petroleum industry
against.role: Industries whose products created much of the Superfund liability and who bore the expired fees
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstatement of Superfund funding taxes after they lapsed in 1995; the fees have remained unrenewed.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan division shows in the record.

industries.note: The reinstated 0.12% corporate environmental tax would fall on these companies, whose products and sites generate much of the Superfund's workload. Their interest in keeping the tax lapsed shifted cleanup costs onto general taxpayers.
A dedicated Superfund revenue stream means more funded cleanup work at contaminated sites. Their business expands as cleanups proceed.
Without the tax, Superfund cleanups at abandoned sites are funded by general revenue — ordinary taxpayers. The bill would relieve them of that share.
